corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Bhumij; Mundari: primary stress on the final syllable if it is heavy, else on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy, else on the penultimate syllable; no information on secondary stress". 714.dq: Hoffmann 1903:4 'In dissyllabic words the accent is generally on the first syllable' (word); Cook 1965:100, rule stated for the MORPHEME: 'This rule applies to stress within morphemes. Stress patterns in words would take further investigation'; Horo et al. 2023:81 'vowel duration clearly does not operate as a word-level cue of prominence ... predictable on the last syllable of a word in isolation'

714.heavy: Cook 1965:100 (the scan; StressTyp2 drops 'of a morpheme'): within a morpheme a closed (CVC) final is stressed, else the penult; p.92 diphthongs /ai au/ 'generally stressed'; in words stress stays on roots. Sinha 1975:39 (carried): CVC.CV initial, else second
714.dflt: Cook: penult (initial in disyllables); Sinha: second syllable; Hoffmann: initial (disyllables); Osada 2008: 2nd/3rd by suffix status
714.prule: Irreconcilable. Cook 1965:100: within a MORPHEME, final if closed (CVC) else penult; word stress 'would take further investigation', tends to stay on roots, formatives unstressed. Sinha 1975:39 (in Horo & Anderson 2021): disyllables 2nd except CVC.CV initial; trisyllables 2nd. Hoffmann 1903:4: disyllables generally initial. Osada 1992: pitch accent; 2008: trisyllables never initial. Horo et al. 2023-25: no robust cue
714.srule: Not mentioned in Hoffmann 1903:4, Cook 1965:92-100 and 286, Horo & Anderson 2021:313-316, Gogoi, Horo & Anderson 2024:86 or Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025:137-150 (the instrumental studies find no robust word-level prominence of any kind). Horo, Gogoi & Anderson 2023:81-82 speak of a 'secondary intensity peak' only as a phonetic peak on the final syllable of 4- and 5-syllable inflected nouns in sentence frames (plus a secondary F0 peak on the second syllable for female speakers), explicitly not a word-level cue. The one Mundari source that states a rhythm is the unpublished Langendoen 1963:15 ms.: main stress on the last accented vowel with 'an alternating (2)1...21 stress pattern' leftward across the word (impressionistic; author unsure how checked vowels affect it).

undet.detail: No single type is licensed. First-hand impressionistic descriptions of the same language give four incompatible stress placements — Hoffmann 1903 (disyllables initial, even with a checked final; accent barely perceptible), Langendoen 1963 (rule-derived, main stress word-final by default, penult keeps accent only before a cluster, final /a/ demoted), Cook 1965…

conflict.would_settle: The instrumental team's announced full analysis (all 10 Khunti speakers, inflected tri- to pentasyllables, and their planned test of Osada 2008's trisyllable/suffix claims) or a perception experiment showing whether Mundari listeners use any word-level prominence at all; if that confirms the null without the current 4-speaker hedge, the record resolves to no-word-stress (or pitch-accent if the second-syllable F0 rise proves categorical). Among unread descriptions, Osada 2008 'Mundari' pp.99-164 (Routledge; digital behind library sign-in, HOLLIS) and Sinha 1975 Mundari Grammar p.39 (CIIL; HathiTrust search-only, Widener PL4559.S49) would upgrade the carried legs to first-hand but, being impressionistic, would not by themselves break the tie; the underlying position-vs-position conflict among Hoffmann/Langendoen/Cook/Sinha is itself unresolved by anything in the copy consulted.

tn.quote: in Mundari disyllables average f0 is higher on the second syllable. However, while the f0 difference is only marginal in words produced in isolation, it is observed to be significantly increased in the words produced in the controlled phrase and sentence frames. This indicates that the declaratives in Mundari can have an initial rising intonation, and that the phrasal and sentential intonations are superseding the f0 contour of the target disyllables. … Thus, the f0 measurements also do not robustly distinguish between prominent and non-prominent syllables in Mundari disyllables.

714.cfw: Hoffmann 1903 reports accent on the first syllable, Cook 1965 a weight-conditioned accent on a closed final syllable and otherwise the penult, Osada 1992 and Sinha 1975 a pitch accent that avoids the first syllable, and the instrumental studies of Horo, Anderson and Gogoi 2023-2025 find no robust acoustic cue to word-level prominence at all, so both the placement and the type of Mundari word prosody remain under active debate among first-hand sources.

715.dq: The main accent of the word is marked as follows: á, é, í, ó, ú Secondary accents are marked as: à, è, ì, ò, ù ... MULTIPLE SYLLABLE WORDS (THREE OR MORE): The last syllable never gets the accent. The last strong syllable nearest to the final syllable gets the main accent.

715.heavy: 'Strong' syllables: long vowels (aa ii oo) and V+h nuclei (ah eh ih oh) are 'naturally strong'; a short vowel 'may be strong if the syllable is formed by a short vowel between two consonants (closed syllable)'; otherwise short-vowel syllables are strong only by position (weak-strong alternation from the left). StressTyp2/Hayes 1985:5 (carried): 'the ordinary heavy/light distinction' i.e. long vowels and closed syllables.
715.dflt: All-short-vowel words alternate weak-strong from the left edge and main stress goes to the rightmost non-final strong syllable (Wulamalúsuw, Pumúsuw); an all-light disyllable is stressed on the second syllable (asún, kpá, apúw).
715.prule: Words of three or more syllables: the final syllable is never accented; the main accent falls on the last strong syllable before the final ('the last strong syllable nearest to the final syllable gets the main accent', usually the penult, else the antepenult). Disyllables: accent the first syllable if it is strong (pámbiil, níisha), otherwise the second (asún, nxáh). Strong = long vowel / Vh, closed short-vowel syllable, or a short-vowel syllable made strong by a preceding weak syllable (weak-strong alternation counted from the word start).
715.srule: Secondary accents (grave: à è ì ò ù) are distinguished from the main accent (acute). Strong syllables (long vowels/Vh, closed short-vowel syllables) are louder, weak ones softer; in runs of short vowels stress alternates weak-strong-weak-strong from the word start (strong-weak-strong-weak when the word begins with a strong syllable; long vowels never weaken; the final syllable is always weak), so the non-final strong syllables before the main accent carry secondary prominence: Wulàmalúsuw /wu-LUH-muh-LISS-oh/, Nòolamálsi /NOO-la-MALsi/, Loohumáasiil /LOW who MAW seal/, Pàyaxkhíikan; words with several long vowels are near-level ('three long syllables each equally stressed before the weak final syllable').

morph.rootq: O'Meara 1990, Appendix to Ch. I, R23-R24 (p.50, verified): 'Final syllables in words of more than two syllables are extrametrical... Any long vowel is metrically strong; any short vowel in a closed syllable is metrically strong; in a sequence of open syllables containing short vowels odd numbered vowels are weak; even numbered vowels are strong... R24. Main Stress Assignment. In words of more than two syllables, penultimate strong syllables receive main stress. If the penultimate syllable is metrically weak, as defined in R23, the antepenultimate syllable is stressed. In disyllabic words the last strong vowel of the word is stressed'…
morph.elicq: O'Meara 1990 p.43, p.2: 'Most of the rules presented here are based upon those given in Goddard (1979a, 1982)... Stress, which is predictable, is not marked (R24)'; 'Although stress is not marked in this study, I give examples to illustrate the effects of R24' (p.50); 'My information on Delaware has been taken primarily from my own field notes, collected at Moraviantown, Ontario during the summers of 1980, 1981, 1984 and 1985.' No statement of whether stress was observed in isolated words, frames or connected speech.…
morph.stmt: Munsee is polysynthetic and predominantly suffixing: all derivation (medials, finals, secondary finals: causative, applicative, passive, reciprocal, nominalisers, verbalisers, diminutive) is suffixal ('Primary derivation forms stems from roots followed by medial and final suffixes. Secondary derivation forms stems from stems by suffixation of finals' - O'Meara 1990 Preface p.x); noun plural/obviative/locative/possessive theme, verbal theme signs, person-number endings, mode (subordinative -n, conjunct endings, subjunctive -e, imperative/prohibitive), negative -(oo)wii and the vestigial aspect markers -p(an)/-sa are all suffixes; the only prefixes are the three person prefixes nə-/kə-/wə…

718.heavy: A long vowel: 'Primary stress falls on a long vowel, wherever it occurs' (Rule 2); a long vowel in the first syllable also blocks the suffixation stress shift (Rule 3a). Closed syllables are not a weight criterion for primary stress (a closed final syllable only conditions even stress across reduplicated roots, p.40).
718.dflt: initial syllable (Rule 1), modulo Rule 3 suffixation shift to the second syllable in suffixed disyllabic nouns
718.prule: Rule 1: stress normally on the first syllable; Rule 2: primary stress falls on a long vowel wherever it occurs (initial/medial long aa takes primary; a word-final long aa takes only secondary, primary staying initial, p.31); Rule 3: suffixed disyllabic nouns shift primary to the second syllable unless the first syllable has a long vowel or the word is interdental-initial with a rhotic after V1; §2.6.2: primary may optionally move to a second syllable with a rhotic/retroflex onset (rr especially).
718.srule: Secondary stress (Oates's ") falls on the penultimate syllable in words of four or more syllables, primary staying initial (Rule 5, stated as a tendency for alternate syllables to carry some stress: 'ngurra"wara 'flood', 'karraka"rranti 'mirage'); reduplications with an open final syllable likewise, with a closed final syllable both roots evenly stressed. Conditioned cases: suffixed verbs/adjectives with coalesced vowels take a second stress on the penult, sometimes equal to or heavier than the first (Rule 4); a rhotic-initial third syllable attracts secondary ('paku"ra); monosyllabic root + disyllabic suffix gives a light final secondary (yan-ti"pu); after a long first-syllable vowel secondary falls on the second syllable ('maan"ku-li); a word-final long aa in a polysyllable carries secondary (p.31).

The foot is a rhythm unit bounded by slight decreases in tempo and including one stressed syllable. Stressed syllables have greater intensity or greater duration, or both, than unstressed syllables of comparable segmental composition. The placement of stress within a foot is…
719.loc: Huttar & Huttar 1972, sections 3-4, pp. 4-6 (stress rule on p. 6); 1994:565 via StressTyp2 entry-627
719.idn: Djuka (Djoeka, Diouka), 'also referred to in the literature as Aukan', creole of eastern Surinam (Cottica and Tapanahonij rivers); informants from Agitiondre (Cottica River), Tottiekamp (lower Saramacca River) and Sara Kreek (near the Tapanahonij); data: 'Field work for this paper was conducted in Paramaribo from…
719.exq_: if there is no long syllable in the stem, stress placement varies freely: the stress may occur on the syllable stressed in the underlying form, or on the first high syllable or all high syllables of the surface form (or on the penult in the case of a surface form with no high syllables)
719.tone: Two underlying tones (high, low) borne by every vowel, with tone sandhi (three surface pitches); the authors adopt tones-plus-sandhi over a pitch-accent analysis because stress is then predictable, and note that prominence by intensity/duration does not always coincide with prominence by pitch; stress falls on the first high-tone syllable when the foot has no long syllable.

morph.rootq: Huttar & Huttar 1972, sec.4 (p.6): 'The placement of stress within a foot is predictable on the basis of the distribution of long and high syllables (defined at the end of 3.) in that foot. If a foot contains a long syllable (and no foot contains more than one long syllable), that syllable is stressed. Otherwise, the first high syllable of the foot is stressed. In feet with only short low syllables, the penultimate syllable is stressed.' The domain is the (tonally defined) foot, which may be polymorphemic: 'All quadrisyllabic feet consist of four short syllables, as in monomorphematic makisita "mosquito" and polymorphematic a-beligi "the mountain"' (p.7). No reference to root or stem vs…
morph.elicq: Huttar & Huttar 1972 p.5: 'We begin with the fact that pitch, intensity, and duration are all phonetic parameters by which Djuka utterances, including stems spoken in isolation, differ.' Frame sentences are used alongside isolation forms: '[ka'misa / na'mo] "just loincloth", [sa'baku / na'mo] "just wading bird", [ta'biki / na'mo] "just island"' (p.5) and 'bubu > bubu in pya bubu de "where is the jaguar?" and in teke waN bubu gi mi "go catch me a jaguar"' (p.7). Fieldwork note (fn.1): 'Field work for this paper was conducted in Paramaribo from December 1968 through March 1969 ... The two principal informants were natives of Agitiondre on the Cottica River.' No instrumental measurements…
morph.stmt: Ndyuka/Nengee is isolating: 'Le nom est un mot invariable (il ne varie ni en genre ni en nombre)' (G&M 2003 p.64); 'En nenge(e), le verbe ne change jamais de forme. Les notions temporelles..., aspectuelles... et celles de la modalite... sont generalement exprimees par des mots independants qui precedent le verbe principal' (p.84); the only bound morphology the grammar describes is derivational and suffixal -- 'le nenge(e) possede des ressources propres pour creer des mots nouveaux, par derivation au moyen de suffixes comme -man, -pe, ou par composition' (p.83) -- plus reduplication (pp.112-113); no prefixes are described.

720.dq: Stress in Nepali words. The rules which determine the position of the stress in Nepali words are complicated. ... The position of the stress depends upon both the length of the vowels and the nature of the syllables in a given word.
720.dloc: Matthews 1984, 'Pronunciation and script', Section 13 'Stress in Nepali words', pp. 17-18; Khatiwada 2009, section 'Stress and pitch' (one sentence); Hayes 1980 MIT pagination pp.108-109.
720.heavy: Vowel length (short a, i, u vs long ā, ī, ū, e, ai, o, au) plus open vs closed syllable: a 'long' penultimate syllable is stressed; the final syllable takes the stress only if it is closed AND contains a long vowel, or ends in two consonants; a final that is open, or closed with a short vowel and a single consonant, does not attract stress.
720.dflt: antepenult in words of 3+ syllables; first (penultimate) syllable in disyllables
720.prule: Right-edge three-syllable window ('last... penultimate... or the antepenultimate'). Disyllables: first syllable stressed when the final is open or closed with a short vowel; final stressed when it is closed and contains a long vowel. Words of three or more syllables: final stressed if closed with a long vowel or ending in two consonants (hin-du-stan, ban-do-bast); otherwise a long penult is stressed (bha-rat-i-ya); otherwise (short penult, light final) the antepenult is stressed (ha-lu-ko). Morphological overrides: plural -haru never stressed, negative na- always stressed, infinitives initial-stressed with stress fixed through most verb forms.

721.dq: Kiparsky 2021 p.417: "A Nez Perce word has a single primary stress, but its constituent morphemes may have lexical accents, from which the stress is calculated compositionally." Aoki 1965 p.10 lists /ˊ/ (stress) as a suprasegmental phoneme separate from /+/ (phonological word juncture), /,/ (pause form) and the terminal contour.
721.dloc: Kiparsky 2021 sec. 3.3 'Stress and accent', p. 417 (section-opening sentence; cf. (47b) p. 423); Aoki 1965 sec. 130 'Suprasegmentals', pp. 10-11 (pp. 67-68 of eScholarship qt0fx0928s; the terminal-contour item is at the top of p. 11)
721.heavy: PRIMARY stress: no weight criterion; Aoki's stress and length phonemes cross-classify (mé·qeʔ vs méqeʔ; wé·cese vs we·cé·se) and Kiparsky 2021: 423 says primary/secondary stresses realize lexical accents 'independently of their bearers' syllable weight and position in the word'; the only weight clause in the primary default is (45c) 'or on its final syllable if it is superheavy' (final -CVVC, 'superheavy (trimoraic)', Kiparsky's own proposal building on Crook 1999: 401, which he reanalyses as disyllabic /-CVV.C/ so that it reduces to the penult default). SECONDARY (rhythmic) stress on unaccented syllables (Crook 1999: 290, 356 via Kiparsky 2021 (46)): heavy = CVV and CVVC (always at least secondary stress) and CVC (secondary stress except word-finally); CV light (stressed only by position: penult obligatorily, initial usually, else optional alternating).
721.dflt: n/a for primary weight; default for words with no lexical accent = penultimate (rightmost non-final) syllable, or the final syllable if it is superheavy -CVVC (Kiparsky 2021 (45c)); monosyllables on the sole syllable.
721.prule: Lexical accent system. Aoki 1965: stress /ˊ/ is a suprasegmental phoneme; verb stems are lexically 'stressed' vs 'unstressed' types with stress-differing allomorphs selected by suffixal environment; some suffixes carry stress; no positional rule is stated. Resolution per Kiparsky 2021 (45), building on Crook 1999 ch. 4: the single primary stress falls (a) on the rightmost DOMINANT accented syllable if any; (b) otherwise on the LEFTMOST accented syllable; (c) otherwise, in words built entirely from accentless morphemes, on the rightmost non-final syllable = penult (or the final syllable if superheavy -CVVC); (d) otherwise on the sole syllable. All nouns are inherently accented; verb stems may be accentless (Crook 1999: 416 via Kiparsky stems paper p. 22).
721.srule: Weight- and position-sensitive secondary stress on inherently unaccented syllables at the Word level (Crook 1999: 290, 356 as stated by Kiparsky 2021 (46)): CVV and CVVC syllables always bear at least secondary stress; CVC syllables bear secondary stress except word-finally; CV syllables are stressed obligatorily in the penult, usually word-initially, otherwise optionally in an alternating pattern. Lexical accents that do not receive the primary surface as secondary stresses. Source status: rests solely on Crook 1999's rules and examples (Kiparsky fn. 24: not marked in any texts, grammars, dictionaries or transcriptions); Aoki 1965 gives no secondary-stress rule; StressTyp2 'No information'.

morph.rootq: Aoki treats stress as a phoneme (§130 p.10: "/'/ (stress) is characterized by high pitch and relative loudness in the syllable") and states no positional rule; his morphology classifies STEMS and SUFFIXES as stressed vs unstressed and lets them compete: §510.1 pp.49-50 "There are three factors determining the allomorphs of general noun stems ... (2) the absence or presence of stress in the affix ... Stress difference is generally characterized by stressed [stem] allomorphs in environments I, II, and III [no affix / unstressed suffix] and [un]stressed allomorphs in IV and V [before a stressed suffix]"; §610.1 p.96 "The two major types of verb stems ... are stressed and unstressed types ...…

722.dq: The stress is always on the next to the last syllable (penultimate), which is the first syllable in most words.
722.heavy: Not stated as 'weight'; the conditioning factor is vowel quality: a penult (first syllable) containing schwa /ə/ may lose stress to the final syllable; all syllables are open (C)V and vowel sequences are heterosyllabic (p.13 item 11), so no CVV/CVC weight exists. (p.13 item 4: schwa 'is usually very short and causes the lengthening of the following consonants'.)
722.dflt: penultimate in the source's framing (all-full-vowel words take penult stress); in StressTyp2's mirror framing (Heavy = full vowel, 'penult if heavy else final') the else-clause is 'final'. The all-schwa case cannot arise because schwa does not occur in the final syllable, so the label is a convention.
722.prule: Stress (non-phonemic) always on the penultimate syllable, which is the first syllable in most (disyllabic) words; stress 'may be shifted' to the last syllable when the first (penultimate) syllable contains a schwa (p.14 béli vs vəlí, zéle vs zəlé; p.13 item 10 bəghá 'to fly' vs 'bágho 'not', ghóbo, ghúbu).
722.srule: No secondary stress rule for native words (one or two syllables; trisyllables rare). For three- or four-syllable borrowings the source tentatively posits a secondary stress on the first syllable (a first-syllable /ə/ becomes /a/, 'probably caused by the placement of a secondary stress'; 'bàláda, kàpála, màradéka, primary on the penult, p.17 Set 7).
722.quote: 12. Stress is not phonemic and it appears as greater vowel length and possibly higher pitch as the spectrograms done by P. Moore and myself as informant at the phonetics lab, University of Michigan (1975) show. The stress is always on the next to the last syllable (penultimate), which is the first syllable in most words. However, the stress may be shifted to the last syllable when the first syllable contains a schwa. Here are some examples: béli 'witness' vəlí 'buy' zéle 'west' zəlé 'eat greedily' 13. The syllable structure of Nga'da is open and mostly of the form (C)V. Words are formed of on…

The word stress always falls on the next to the last syllable (penultimate), which is the first syllable in most words. However, the stress may be shifted to the last syllable if the first syllable contains schwa. Monosyllabic particles as well as cliticised particles are normally unstressed.'…

Moore and myself as informant at the phonetics laboratory, The University of Michigan (Fall 1975).' (The 1977 NUSA version, p.14: 'as the spectrograms done by P. Moore and myself as informant at the phonetics lab, University of Michigan (1975) show.') Whether the spectrograms were of isolated words or words in frames is not stated; the placement rule itself rests on the author's native-speaker knowledge (p.114: 'my own personal intuition as a speaker of Ngadha (which is my first language)').
morph.stmt: Radically isolating: 'Ngadha has no morphology apart from a few cliticised particles. Tense, gender and plurality are not marked, and most of the syntax of the language is taken care of by word order' (Djawanai 1983 p.113; cf. 1977 p.14 'There is no derivational or inflectional morphology in Nga'da'). The few bound elements are overwhelmingly post-host enclitics (discourse pointer -na, perfect -gha, imperative -si/-to/-setto, multiword formators -nea/-pii), the one pre-host bound form being the numeral sa- 'one' (sa-eko 'one-CLASS.ANIMAL'); grammatical particles (da, vi, go, nga, mu, negator bha'i) are free, mostly pre-head, unstressed monosyllables; derivation is limited to compounding…

722.sec_rule: Secondary stress on the initial syllable of three- and four-syllable words (Indonesian loans; native words are mono- or disyllabic and carry one stress), primary on the penult: 'bàláda 'Dutch', 'bàdéra 'flag', gàréja, jàbáta, kàpála, pàmaréta, màradéka; given (hedged 'probably') as the cause of first-syllable /ə/ > /a/ in such words.
722.sec_quote: Set 7. /ə/ is substituted by /a/ when it occurs in the first syllable of a three or four-syllable word. This is probably caused by the placement of a secondary stress. Examples: belanda 'bàláda 'Dutch'; bendera 'bàdéra 'flag'; gereja gàréja 'church'; jembatan jàbáta 'bridge'; kepala kàpála 'head, chief'; pemerentah pàmaréta 'government'; merdeka màradéka 'free', 'independent'

723.dq: Stress operates on two levels - word and phrase. For the purpose of the present Grammar a "word" is to be defined as a free form consisting of one or more morphemes, such that it can be given in citation. ... 2.1. Stress on Single Morpheme Words ... 2.2. Stress on Polymorphemic Words ... 2.3. Phrasal Stress
723.dloc: Capell, A. (1970). Section 2: Stress and intonation, in Coate & Oates 1970, p. 7 (Section 2 opening paragraph; word stress 2.1-2.2 pp. 7-8 vs 'Phrasal Stress' 2.3 p. 8) [archive.org scan fragments of the restricted scans]; Rumsey 1982:59 (postpositions bear independent second-degree stress)
723.heavy: a long vowel in a subsequent (non-initial) syllable of a monomorphemic word 'tends to attract stress' away from the default first syllable; vowel length only (Capell: 'not generally phonemic'); closed syllables not mentioned
723.dflt: initial syllable (of the monomorphemic word / root)
723.prule: Monomorphemic words: stress on the first syllable unless a subsequent syllable has a long vowel, which then 'tends to attract stress' (a long first syllable keeps the stress in any case); prefixation does not alter stress; polymorphemic words stress the root morpheme; noun suffixes do not advance stress, verb suffixes may, and certain enclitic suffixes (-di, emphatic -dju, indirect-object markers on the -ma- auxiliary) move it a syllable forward; the number of syllables determines an even-syllable (CvCvCvCv) vs odd-syllable (CvCvCv) stress pattern whose stress marks are not recoverable from the scan read here; StressTyp2, compiled from the page, reports the four-syllable pattern as penultimate primary with initial secondary (its example ˌnjaŋaˈruŋgun, which Capell glosses 'prefix with weak stress attached to root; -ruŋgun with stress on first syllable').
723.srule: Capell marks main, secondary and weak stress. Word: syllable-count parity sets the pattern (even CvCvCvCv, odd CvCvCv; the stress marks on these schematics are lost in the accessible scan); his 4-syllable example njaŋaruŋgun has weak stress on the prefix and main stress on the root-initial penult (StressTyp2's 'penultimate stress and initial secondary stress'). Phrasal verbs: the auxiliary carries main stress, the invariable root only secondary; a disyllabic pronominal suffix (-naŋga) and encliticised demonstratives take at most a secondary stress (§2.3). Postpositions always bear second-degree stress; a cliticised possessive pronoun takes secondary stress (Rumsey 1982:59, 70). No rule for words of five or more syllables is stated.
723.quote: Words consisting of a single morpheme are stressed on the first syllable unless there is a long vowel in a subsequent syllable. While vowel length is not generally phonemic in Ngarinjin, there are certain cases where stress plus length of vowel must be regarded as so ... In words of this type a syllable containing a long vowel tends to attract stress. Of course, if the first syllable is long stress will fall on it in any case ... Prefixation does not alter stress ... A suffix also does not advance the stress ... In the case of the verb, however, a suffix may advance the stress ... The basic s…
723.loc: Capell in Coate & Oates 1970:7-8, Section 2.1 'Stress on Single Morpheme Words' and 2.2 'Stress on Polymorphemic Words' (enclitics p. 8); Rumsey 1982:9 fn.1, 59

723.exq_: addition of morphemes to a root does not move the stress, though in a few cases this statement does not hold. ... when -di is added ... it serves as an enclitic, moving the stress a syllable forward ... other suffixes act as enclitics and advance the stress a syllable, e.g. the emphatic -dju

724.dq: When there are both high and low tones in a word, the pattern is more complicated. The last high tone gets main stress.
724.heavy: high-toned syllable (the stress-attracting property is HIGH TONE, not vowel length or coda; ST1 note: ': high tone'). Not opened at quote grade: Enrico 2003 Haida Syntax p.13 (seen only via Wikipedia paraphrase) reportedly says unmarked heavy syllables (long vowel or sonorant coda) carry high pitch and unmarked light syllables low pitch, so quantity feeds tone which feeds stress, with lexically marked tone exceptions.
724.prule: Main stress on the last (rightmost) high-toned syllable of the word; in words with level tone (no high/low contrast), main stress on the final syllable.
724.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables before the main stress; when the main stress (last high-toned syllable) is not word-final, the final syllable and alternate syllables before it also carry secondary stress. Secondary placement ignores tone (de Lacy 2007:300, restating Enrico 1991).
724.quote: Enrico 1991:111-121 (as carried by StressTyp2): "In level tone words, the pattern is simple. The final syllable gets main stress and all alternates before it get secondary stress. When there are both high and low tones in a word, the pattern is more complicated. The last high tone gets main stress. All alternates before it and the last syllable and alternates before it get secondary stress." | de Lacy 2002:23, (32): "(32) lists a number of languages in which tone is the primary factor in determining the position of stress ... b. Stress the rightmost high-toned syllable, else the rightmost syl…
724.idn: Cited description is of the Masset (Haida Gwaii) dialect of Northern Haida ('Masset Haida' in both Enrico 1991's title and de Lacy 2002 (32b)); the rule is not asserted for the Alaskan (Kaigani) dialect.
724.tone: Word-level high vs low tone (Enrico: 'level tone words' vs words with 'both high and low tones'); tone is the property that places main stress (de Lacy 2002: 'tone is the primary factor in determining the position of stress'); secondary stress is by alternating count.

726.heavy: Long vowels; closed syllables (ST1 note carried with the Hayes 1995 passage). Primary definition, Freeland 1951:6 sec.6: 'All those syllables are long which contain a long vowel, or a short vowel that is followed by a long consonant, or a combination of two consonants. Any consonant occurring before another, then, though short in itself, must be regarded as long from the point of view of syllabic length'; his composition table counts 'short cons. plus short v. plus short cons. (final pos.)' as short and 'short cons. plus long v. plus short cons. (only in final position)' as long, i.e. a word-final short-vowel CVC is light. Corroborated for Northern Sierra by Kroeber 1911:279: 'It seems that long vowels and vowels followed by a glottal stop or doubled consonant generally bear the accent, which is well marked.'
726.dflt: peninitial (second syllable), which is then lengthened so that one of the first two syllables is always heavy on the surface
726.prule: Stress the initial syllable if it is heavy (CVV or CVC); otherwise stress the second syllable, which then surfaces long (iambic lengthening), so the initial disyllabic foot is light-unstressed + heavy-stressed.
726.srule: Secondary stress falls most frequently on the word-final syllable: present in three-syllable nouns and verb forms with initial major stress and normally in longer nouns; absent in three-syllable nouns with second-syllable major stress; a final case suffix is unstressed; in longer verb forms it falls on a final syllabic pronominal suffix, otherwise on certain suffix syllables (-ànï- distant past, -ìšï- usitative, -tànï-); a secondary stress immediately after the major stress is not usual in this dialect (vocatives and volitionals only; frequent in Southern Sierra). Noticeable in short phrases, fading in running narrative. No alternating rhythm is described.
726.quote: The initial syllable is stressed if it is heavy, otherwise the second syllable is stressed. Any initial disyllabic foot necessarily takes the canonical form short unstressed + long stressed. An alternating length pattern, possibly indicating iterative iambic footing, is noted. (Hayes 1995:261, StressTyp2 passage 1457) ... 728.dq: The prosodic head is the syllable bearing main stress and the constraint NonFinality is therefore understood to mean that a word-final syllable does not bear main stress.
728.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic syllable: either a long (bimoraic) vowel or a short vowel plus a moraic coda consonant (geminate/cluster); non-final syllables are maximally bimoraic (V: with no coda, or V + one coda C). A word-final single consonant is non-moraic (syllabified as onset of a catalectic syllable), so a final syllable counts as heavy/stressable only when its vowel is long (surface V:C, or lexically long final V as in alle, kafe) or it is closed by a geminate/cluster (VCC) -- Rice (1999, via StressTyp2) calls these final 'superheavy' syllables.
728.dflt: penult ('When an input lacks any bimoraic vowels or moraic consonants, then the grammar will select as optimal candidates in which stress appears on the penult', sec.5.2 p.22)
728.prule: Main stress is right-edge oriented (AlignRight) with NonFinality >> AlignRight keeping it off a word-final open syllable; stressed syllables must be heavy (bimoraic) and unstressed ones light (two-way implication). A word-final consonant is a non-moraic onset to a catalectic syllable and buffers NonFinality, so consonant-final words take FINAL stress by default (tomát with lengthened vowel from an input with no moraic specification; trafíkk, agúrk with an input-moraic final C) and PENULTIMATE stress only when the penult is underlyingly heavy (éddik: moraic medial C; kókos, bóraks: bimoraic penult vowel). Vowel-final words take penultimate stress by default (bikíni; native disyllables: heavy stressed initial + light schwa final, tape/tappe), FINAL stress only when the final vowel is bimoraic in the input (kafé, allé), and ANTEPENULTIMATE stress when the antepenult vowel is bimoraic in the input and the last two syllables are light (Amérika), *Clash barring an additional penult foot. Placement is thus decided partly by lexical moraic specification ('determined in part by faithfulness'); the default/'native' pattern is penultimate; antepenult loans vary by speaker (narkotika).
728.srule: Not mentioned in Rice 2006 (ROA-747 ms, secs.1-6 read; main stress only). 729.dq: This chapter discusses the position of stress in isolated words. The syllable which is stressed in an isolated word is the same one which is stressed when that particular word is the most prominent one within a sequence of words (see Chapters 5 and 23). ... The conditions determining sentence stress, i.e. which particular word within a sentence is to be stressed, are discussed in Chapter 23.
729.dloc: Goksel & Kerslake 2005 ch. 4 'Word stress', sec. 4.1.1-4.1.2 (pp. 26-28) and sec. 4.3-4.3.1 (pp. 29-30); Inkelas 1994 ROA-39 pp. 5-6: sec. 3.1 ex. (9)-(10) and secondary-stress fn. on p. 5, sec. 3.2 ex. (12) ('stress is unfailingly final') on p. 6.
729.heavy: Goksel & Kerslake state no weight criterion at all (regular stress is final regardless of syllable shape; non-final stress is lexical, 'indicated in dictionary entries'). Only for the lexical subclass of place names and some borrowings ('Sezer stems') does Inkelas 1994 (after Sezer 1981) state a weight rule; H there = closed syllables and long-vowel syllables per the grouped examples (Is.tán.bul, An.tál.ya, Hak.kâ:.ri...H; A.dá.na, Ke.né.di...L L), 'the weight of the final syllable is irrelevant'. StressTyp2 entry likewise: ': Long vowels; closed syllables'.
729.dflt: not applicable to the regular rule (always final); within Sezer stems: penult (e.g. A.dá.na)
729.prule: Regular word stress on the final syllable of the word; stressable suffixes carry stress to the new final syllable (kitáp, kitap-lár, kitaplar-ím, kitaplarım-dá). Weight plays no role in the regular rule.
729.srule: None described for regular (finally stressed) words: Göksel & Kerslake 2005 mark one stress per isolated word and use 'secondary stress' only for sentence-level prominence; Inkelas & Orgun 2003: 'only one stress per word'. The existence of word-level secondary stress is disputed and left unanalysed (Inkelas 1994: 'Secondary stress in Standard Turkish is controversial'; Özçelik 2014 fn. 4). Özçelik 2014/2017 transcribes a variable secondary stress only in words with two exceptional (pre-stressing or stressed) suffixes, on the head of the non-initial foot (dinlé-me-dì-de, bek(léme)(dìde)).

morph.rootq: §4.1.1: 'Most roots in Turkish (including all polysyllabic verbal roots and some loan words) are stressable on the final syllable.' §4.3: 'In terms of stress, the suffixes of Turkish are divided into two classes: stressable and unstressable.' §4.3.1 (i): 'When a stressable suffix is added to a root in which the final syllable (whether part of the root, or itself a suffix) is also stressable, the position of word stress moves to the new final syllable' (kitáp, kitap-lár, kitaplar-ím ...); (ii): 'When a stressable suffix is added to a root in which the final syllable is not stressable (4.1.2), i.e. is irregular, the position of word stress remains on the stressed syllable of the root'…
morph.elicq: Ch. 4 intro: 'The term stress refers to the high pitch and loudness with which a syllable is pronounced relative to others in the same word or sequence of words. This chapter discusses the position of stress in isolated words. The syllable which is stressed in an isolated word is the same one which is stressed when that particular word is the most prominent one within a sequence of words (see Chapters 5 and 23). In this chapter an acute accent will be used to indicate a stressed syllable.' (No instrumental measurements or frame-sentence procedure are mentioned; the description is a reference-grammar statement about citation forms.)
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: 'The main word formation process in Turkish is suffixation, the formation of a new word by attaching an affix to the right of a root' (ch. 6 intro); 'In Turkish, because of its highly agglutinative structure, the description of word structure is largely a matter of identifying the different categories of suffixes... and in what order' (Introduction); 'Apart from the reduplicative prefixes discussed in Chapter 9 [emphatic kap-kara type], the only prefixes Turkish has are of foreign origin... tn.quote: The intonational contour of a Turkish declarative sentence produced in a neutral context typically consists of a sequence of rising tones [L H], followed by a nuclear accented word in a narrower pitch range, and a low boundary tone at the end of the sentence. The domain of a rising tone is a Prosodic Word (PW) with the L tone on the first syllable of a word and the H tone on its stressed syllable, often the last syllable of the word. ... In Ipek and Jun’s [3] intonation model, a High tone on a stressed syllable is analyzed as a H* pitch accent regardless of the location of stress
tn.cite: Ipek, Canan & Sun-Ah Jun. 2014. Distinguishing phrase-final and phrase-medial high tone on finally stressed words in Turkish. In N. Campbell, D. Gibbon & D. Hirst (eds.), Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2014 (Dublin), 393-397. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2014-66
tn.locator: p. 393, sec. 1 Introduction, first and third paragraphs
tn.note: Intonation study: each prosodic word has a postlexical [L H] rise, H* on the stressed (usually final) syllable, H*-/LH- at phrase edges. Lexical tone neither claimed nor denied; stress presupposed.

729.cfw: Göksel & Kerslake 2005, Inkelas & Orgun 2003, Özçelik 2014 and 2017, Bodur et al. 2021 and Hagberg 1993 all put regular Turkish stress on the final syllable of the fully suffixed word, weight-insensitive and with only lexically or morphologically marked exceptions, and they differ only on whether that final prominence is metrical stress or an intonational boundary tone.

730.heavy: Source states no weight criterion: long vowels and vowel glides are analysed as two syllables (V.V), so stress is penultimate by syllable(=vowel) count; CVC syllables occur in all positions with no stress effect mentioned. Secondary stress on words longer than three syllables occurs on the first syllable.' -- stated over the phonological word, with affixal syllables counted (e.g. /"u.ru.ra.tu.a.'na.vu/ 'will surely fish', stress on a suffix syllable; Waryengsi et al. 1987 p.14 'U-ru-ra-tu-an-A-vu'). Morphology is mentioned only as exceptions: Peckham 1991 §3.1 (p.118) 'There are morphophonological exceptions which allow an antepenultimate stress or a word final CVV. These involve an object marker /-i/'; §2.2.4 'The same syllable that was stressed in the full form is…
morph.elicq: No explicit elicitation protocol is stated. The description rests on stress-marked citation forms (Peckham 1991 §2.1: 'The following examples are written phonemically', isolated words with stress marks) together with observations of fast/connected speech: §2.2.4 'In fast speech, Mairasi speakers tend to abbreviate words which end with a vowel. ... The same syllable that was stressed in the full form is stressed in the abbreviated form, even though it is no longer penultimate'; §3.2 'Although, in isolation, words may end with a vowel; in fast speech, the same words are closed by consonants'. No instrumental measurements.
morph.stmt: Peckham 1982 p.75: 'In keeping with the fact that SOV is the normal word order in the Mairasi clause, extensive use is made of suffixes' and p.89: 'As mentioned earlier, Mairasi verbs make more use of suffixes than prefixes' -- verb template (I.O.-prefix) STEM-SUBJECT-D.O.-I.O.-MODE-ASPECT(-NEG), motion verbs SUBJECT.prefix-STEM-DIRECTION-MODE-ASPECT (Tables 11-12 pp.90-91); the only prefixes are the person set o-/ne-/na-/ee-/e-/ne- (inalienable possessor on nouns; subject/experiencer on a closed class of motion, stative and perception verbs; object on three perception verbs) and the animate-agreement n(a)-/ne- on adjectives; nominal case is suffixal/postpositional.

tn.quote: There are two contrastive pitch levels³. They contrast only on stressed syllables, which normally take a higher pitch than nonstressed or secondarily stressed syllables. Thus the contrast manifests itself when the stressed syllable of one word is higher than the stressed syllable of the word with which it contrasts. This represents an incomplete system remotely akin to that of the Ekagi language 150 km to the east (Doble 1961:152-155). ... [ʔa'ƀó:] 'close' [ʔ'ƀò:] 'soon' ['ʔandá] 'branch' ['ʔndà] 'pants' ... [note 3] Only twelve minimal pairs of contrasting pitch have been found to date.

tn.note: Two contrastive pitch levels (high, low) that contrast only on the stressed (penultimate) syllable; called an incomplete system, rare, twelve minimal pairs known; pitch not written in the orthography.

731.dq: Stress in words of more than one syllable lies as a rule on the syllabic preceding the last consonant of the word
731.heavy: a syllable 'closed by a consonant' (only nasals and the semivowels j, w may close a syllable, so Vj/Vw sequences count as closed); in addition an open penult 'in ə' is too light to keep stress when the antepenult is closed (implicit scale closed > open full vowel > open ə). Vowel length is not phonemic ('The relevant element is this stress, not length').
731.prule: Stress lies 'as a rule on the syllabic preceding the last consonant of the word' = final syllable if consonant-closed, otherwise penult; in 3-4-syllable vowel-final words with a closed antepenult and an open ə penult, stress 'tends to shift' to the antepenult.
731.srule: Secondary stress on the 2nd syllable and, in long words, on every other even-numbered syllable (counted from the left edge); quantity-sensitive: on the 1st syllable instead if it is heavy (nasal-closed or diphthong, incl. closed ə-syllables) or if the 2nd is an open ə-syllable; heavy syllables may stay unstressed next to another stress, clashes do occur, and at most two adjacent syllables are unstressed, so surface intervals are binary or ternary (Elenbaas 1999:58-60, own fieldwork). Earlier formulation in the primary source, Cowan 1965:9: 'a secondary stress affecting the 3rd syllable forward from the main stress, or the 2nd syllable forward if this is closed by a consonant' (ha,bəwdo'koke;ədəka'wale).

morph.rootq: Basic rule is word-phonological, not root-based (II.4.1 p.9): 'Stress in words of more than one syllable lies as a rule on the syllabic preceding the last consonant of the word, e.g., ˈjoku, "dog"; ˈmijɛ, "woman"; ... əˈdəke, "he saw" (aorist); ˈhojbo, "kill!"; uˈkəwnə, "he told him"; məˈkajde, "they came"; but: faˈləm, "head" ... hodoˈbom "let me kill".' (suffixes regularly carry stress). The root is invoked only for a class of deviations (p.10): 'Verbal roots of more than one syllable ending in -ə preceded by one of the consonants admissible as finals, tend to treat this consonant as root final and drop the -ə, when an affix, beginning with a consonant, follows. The stress then remains…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined; the description rests on the author's fieldwork and is illustrated with isolated citation forms carrying stress marks: 'It was the result of fieldwork during my stay in West New Guinea in the years 1946-1950 ... this fieldwork could only be done to the extent that official civil service duties permitted. But during a further term of service, which finally ended in 1956, I had the opportunity of collecting more data concerning the language' (I.1 p.1); 'We shall indicate such irregularities of stress by a high dash preceding the stressed syllable (a low dash means a secondary stress)' (II.4.1 p.10). Impressionistic; no instrumental data, no frame…
morph.stmt: Almost exclusively suffixing: 'A verbal form consists of one or two verbal roots to which may be added affixes for person (including number) both for the subject and the object (direct or indirect), mood, tense and aspect. The only prefix in use is the negative ə-.' (III.4 p.18); cf. III.1 p.11: 'prefixation to verbal roots of the negative prefix ə- (unique case); affixation, by which we understand the adding to the verbal structure of all flexional elements which follow the root'. Nouns are uninflected ('Flexion is limited to the verb, the personal pronouns, and a few near relationship terms', III.3 p.15); relational marking is by enclitic postpositions, possession by preposed (proclitic)…

evidence_works.detail: Sentani, after Cowan 1965 and Hayes 1995, is the quantity-sensitive example of ternary iteration: final if heavy, else penult, with further stresses every third syllable leftwards and on heavy syllables unless that makes a clash. 732.heavy: a long vowel in the first syllable ('if the first syllable involves a long vowel, then it must receive primary stress'); contrastive vowel length exists only in the word-initial syllable (p.437); closed syllables play no role
732.dflt: first syllable if the word has an even number of syllables (2,4), second syllable if odd (3,5)
732.prule: (1) an initial syllable with a long vowel takes primary stress; (2) if the word has no long vowel, primary stress falls on the first syllable in di- and quadrisyllabic words and on the second syllable in tri- and quinquesyllabic words (rules stated to be identical to Wargamay's). 732.srule: Secondary stress falls on the syllable next but one after the primary stress, except that a final syllable can never bear stress (e.g. bíyaḏàla 'water snake': primary on the 1st, secondary on the 3rd syllable; none in ḏíŋa, bulbíri, ŋú:ḏu, ḏí:baɽi, where the candidate syllable is final or absent).

morph.stmt: §1.1 p.431: 'Nyawaygi is a fairly typical Australian language with a suffixing, agglutinative structure and free word order.'; §2.2 p.441: 'Since Nyawaygi is an entirely suffixing language... all long vowels occur in roots; affixes exclusively involve short vowels.' Every item in the chapter's List of Affixes (pp.524-5) is a suffix; person is carried by free pronouns, negation and modality partly by free preverbal particles (biya(y) 'not', mali 'don't', gapul 'perhaps').

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Obokuitai; Obogwitai; Baburiwa: primary stress on the right-most heavy syllable, else on final syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Stress on the syllable with the highest pitch in the word; if two or more syllables share the highest pitch, the one closest to the end of the word; if all syllables carry the same pitch, the last syllable. — StressTyp2's L/L 'right-most heavy syllable, else final' reproduces the source's positional logic exactly, but its 'heavy' is pitch height (ST1: extra-high > high > low), not syllable quantity, so the 'weight-sensitive' pool label is true only in the prominence-driven sense; StressTyp2's carried passage matches p. 86…

733.dq: Stress occurs on the last syllable of a word if the same pitch is on all syllables. In a word with various pitches, stress occurs on the highest pitch.
733.dloc: sec. 5.4.2 'Stress', p. 86; sec. 5 'Suprasegmentals', p. 81; sec. 4.1 'The Syllable', p. 77; sec. 4.4.1 'Vowel Length', p. 81
733.heavy: Pitch height, not quantity: the stressed syllable is the one bearing the highest pitch in the word (high /1/, realised extra-high [1'] on /i/; falling /12/; low /2/); ties go to the rightmost; all-same-pitch words stress the final syllable. Vowel length and coda /k/ play no stated role; every syllable is 'one mora of timing'.
733.dflt: final syllable (when all syllables carry the same pitch)
733.prule: Stress on the syllable with the highest pitch in the word; if two or more syllables share the highest pitch, the one closest to the end of the word; if all syllables carry the same pitch, the last syllable.
733.srule: Not mentioned in Jenison & Jenison 1991 (sec. 5 'Suprasegmentals', pp. 81-87, incl. 5.4.2 'Stress' p. 86; whole article pp. 69-90): the stress section places a single stress per word by pitch height and speaks only of stressed vs 'unstressed syllables'.

733.idn: Obokuitai, the language of the village of Obokui (Lakes Plain region, northern Irian Jaya); the source notes the language of these groups was initially labeled 'Baburiwa'; data: Village of Obokui (about 110 of approximately 125 speakers; the rest at Biri, Kustera, Haya), Lakes Plain region of northern Irian Jaya…
733.exq_: Stress occurs on the last syllable of a word if the same pitch is on all syllables. In a word with various pitches, stress occurs on the highest pitch. In a word with two pitches of the same height which are the highest in the word, stress occurs on the syllable closest to the end of the word.
733.tone: Obokuitai has contrastive pitch: two level pitches /1/ (high) and /2/ (low) and a falling /12/, with minimal pairs (sec. 5.4.1); stress placement is derived from pitch (highest-pitched syllable, rightmost if tied, final syllable if all pitches are the same).

734.dq: Sauzet 2001:5 'L'occitan accentue la fin du mot: la syllabe finale ou la pénultième.' (Sauzet further distinguishes 'l'accent de mot' from 'l'accent de syntagme', p.8); Wheeler's statement is about word shapes (proparoxytones/paroxytones, consonant-final words).
734.dloc: Wheeler 1988 p.251, section 'Stress', running head 'OCCITAN 251'; Sauzet 2001 HAL preprint p.5; Sauzet 2025 p.2
734.heavy: A word-final consonant (closed final syllable) attracts stress to the ultima, unless that consonant is an inflectional morpheme (plural -s, verbal -n/-m etc.); no vowel-length contrast. StressTyp2/Roca remark: 'heavy ultimas are always stressed... closed syllables are still heavy in Occitan'.
734.prule: Two-syllable right-edge window (no proparoxytones except Nicart/Italian varieties): stress is final when the word ends in a non-inflectional consonant (consonant-final paroxytones 'rare': angel, credit, Antibol), otherwise penultimate in vowel-final words; vowel-final oxytones exist as lexically/orthographically marked items (e.g. aquò [akˈɔ]); in verbs stress placement is morphologised (inflectional -s/-n/-m do not count: dison, cantàvam, sabon 'they know' vs sabon 'soap').
734.srule: Wheeler 1988:251 gives no secondary stress for simple words (his only secondary marks are in verb+enclitic groups, ˌparla-ˈli / doˈnatz-ˌme -- see domain note). Sichel-Bazin 2015 (instrumental): below the Accentual Phrase Occitan has primary stress at the Prosodic Word and secondary stress at the foot level; secondary stresses follow a binary leftward parse from the primary-stressed syllable (feet may cross word boundaries onto clitics) and the word-initial syllable carries secondary stress; their tonal marking is optional (mainly AP-initial rises), rhythmic accents being restricted to certain speech styles.
734.quote: [Wheeler 1988:251] Except in Nice and varieties in Italy where, e.g. mànega 'sleeve', diménegue 'Sunday', 'parla-li 'speak to him', are to be found, Occitan shuns proparoxytones, and shifts stress to a following syllable, to give, for example, paroxytonic lagrema 'tear', persegue 'peach', silaba 'syllable', classica 'classical (f.)', credula 'credulous (f.)'. Occitan shuns proparoxytones, and shifts stress to a following syllable, to give, for example, paroxytonic lagrema 'tear', persegue 'peach', silaba 'syllable' ... Unless a final consonant is an inflectional morpheme (e.g. joves 'young people', dison 'they say', cantavam 'we sang') consonant-final paroxytones are rare. ... Post-clitic pronouns are now stressed: parla-'li 'speak to him', do'natz-'me 'give me'.' Morphology-referring statements (p.263-264): 'The first and second person plural endings are stressed in the present and future paradigms. The past (including prospective-in-past/conditional)…
morph.elicq: Wheeler 1988 p.246-247: 'In what follows, we adopt a basically diasystemic, and somewhat abstract, approach to the phonological system. This is intended as a key to understanding what is going on in Occitan as a whole, rather than as a strict phonological analysis of any one dialect' -- a compiled handbook description; no elicitation method, speakers, frames or measurements are mentioned for the stress statement (p.251). Sauzet 2025 illustrates stress only with isolated minimal pairs and one two-word phrase: 'sabon [s'abu(n)] 'ils savent' et sabon [sab'u(n)] 'savon', Empacha aquo [empatʃak'ɔ] 'il empeche ca' Empachaca [empatʃ'akɔ] 'il empetre''.
morph.stmt: Wheeler describes Occitan inflection and derivation as entirely post-stem: verb forms are stem + theme vowel + tense/aspect/mood + person-number endings ('Combinations of Theme Vowels with Person/Number Inflections'; 'Structure of Verb Inflection': Inf. a+r, Gerund a+nt, Ptcp. a+d, Past imperf. av+H, Past perf. pret.stem+'er+F, p.262), nominals take gender -e/-a and plural '/+s/ suffixed to each element of the NP' (p.255-256), and word formation uses 'freely usable suffixes' (-et, -ot, -on, -el, -as/-assa, -aire/-eire, -ejar, p.277); the only pre-stem grammatical material is proclitic -- object/reflexive pronouns…

736.dq: [p.91] In both KA and CA, word-final accented feet have two variants: a stressed form in which the word-final accented syllable is distinctly stressed and pitch is elevated as with non-final accented syllables, and a destressed form in which the word-final accented syllable is destressed ... The stressed variant of the word-final foot is found mainly in connected speech and before a "thinking" pa…
736.dloc: sec. 1.2 p.82 (weight); sec. 1.4 PA-rule 4 p.91 (stress); sec. 3.1 p.107; FD-rule IC p.110; FD-rule IIB p.112; sec. 3.4 pp.114-115 (IIIA heavy foot, IIIB2 iambic foot); sec. 3.5 p.116 (lexical exceptions)
736.heavy: Heavy = syllable containing two full vowels (vowel pair, i.e. long vowel or diphthong); a single-vowel syllable is light whether open or closed, EXCEPT that a word-initial light closed syllable is defined as an accented foot (FD-rule IC), so CVC counts for accent only word-initially. Phonetic vowel length is derived (iambic lengthening, compression), hence Leer's terms light/heavy rather than short/long.
736.dflt: All-light word with open initial syllable: syllables 1-2 form an iambic foot with accent on the 2nd syllable (FD-rule IIIB2); thereafter, in CA, 'FD-rules IIC and IIIB2 alternate uniformly throughout the word subsequent to initial stress assignment' (p.114), i.e. accent roughly every third syllable in light strings, a single light syllable before word boundary being an unaccented foot (IIB) and a leftover LL pair an iamb accented on its last syllable. Source examples (sec. 3.4.3, p.116): ataka [a.ta:.ka] 'my father' (a.tá | ka); ternary spacing in a light string shown by atmakutartuten 'you're going to backpack' (CA) [at | ma | ku.tax | tu.ten] (initial at- accented by IC, ma an unaccented foot by IIC). (In KA the post-initial rhythm additionally depends on 'accent-advancing' syllables, sec. 4.)
736.prule: Feet are defined left to right in cycles; the final (or only) syllable of every accented foot is accented (=stressed). First cycle (identical in Koniag KA and Chugach CA): an initial heavy (CVV) syllable is an accented heavy foot (IIIA); an initial light closed syllable (including one closed by e-deletion IA or automatic gemination IB before a heavy syllable) is an accented light foot (IC); otherwise the first two light syllables form an iambic foot with accent on the second (IIIB2). So the first stress is on syllable 1 if it is CVV or CVC, else on syllable 2. Leer does not rank one stress as primary over the others.
736.srule: No stress is ranked as primary: Leer assigns the same stress to the final (or only) syllable of every accented foot (PA-rule 4 'Stress is assigned to accented syllables'; 'equally prominent stresses' Martinez-Paricio & Kager 2016 sec.2.1; no acoustic culminativity, Alden 2023 ch.4), so the 'primary' shown is simply the first stress. After the first foot, feet are built left to right: a heavy CVV syllable is a foot and stressed (IIIA); a single light syllable before a heavy syllable or word end is skipped (IIB); a light syllable before two lights is skipped (IIC); two lights form an iamb stressed on the second (IIIB2) - in Chugach 'IIC and IIIB2 alternate uniformly throughout the word subsequent to initial stress assignment' (stress on every third syllable in light strings), heavy syllables interrupting. Lesser degree of stress only in Koniag: non-final skipped light syllables are weakly stressed and may be raised in pitch (PA-rule 5); in Chugach they are unstressed (PA-rule 6). Word-final stressed syllables may be destressed utterance-finally.

dqtr.text: the main stress falls on the heaviest syllable of the last three syllables of the word (§22.2.2); cf. §22.1.3 'the level of the word is an important notion of Pirahã phonology. However, we have not yet arrived at a satisfactory definition of this level in phonological terms. Therefore, we refer here only to the word as a lexico-syntactic unit.'

737.dq: a acentuação principal recai na sílaba mais pesada das últimas três sílabas da palavra (§22.2.2); cf. §22.1.3 'o nível da palavra é uma noção importante da fonologia pirahã. Porém, não temos chegado ainda a uma definição satisfatória deste nível em termos fonológicos. Portanto, nos referimos aqui apenas à palavra como unidade léxico-sintática.'
737.heavy: Five syllable types CVV, GVV, VV, CV, GV (C = voiceless consonant, G = voiced consonant); syllable weight derives from the number of vowels in the syllable AND the relative duration of the onset consonant: voiceless consonants are [+tense] and therefore 'heavier' than voiced ones. I.e. a weight scale combining vowel count (VV vs V) with onset presence/voicing; no codas exist.
737.dflt: No quantity-insensitive default as such: if the last three syllables are all of the same type, the tie-break puts stress on the rightmost, i.e. the final syllable (e.g. bi.'gí GV GV).
737.prule: Main stress falls on the heaviest syllable among the last three syllables of the word; when the heaviest syllable type present in the last three syllables occurs more than once there, the rightmost such token is stressed.
737.srule: Not mentioned in Everett 1983 (sect. 22.1.3-22.2.3, pp. 199-203, and sect. 22.3.3.3, pp. 215-218 read: only 'acentuação principal' is described). Later first-hand statement (Everett 1986 = pre-publication of Everett 1988 NLLT): none within the word -- words and lexical compounds 'have a single, primary stress'; 'secondary stresses arise only in syntactically formed compounds but not in lexical compounds', i.e. in postlexically fused noun+adjective / noun+verb phrases each component keeps a stress (the lighter one deleted when both fall in one ternary foot).
737.quote: 22.2.1. Tipos silábicos. Em KE (1978) e Everett (1979; 1981); (em preparação), cinco tipos silábicos foram descritos no pirahã. ... Estes tipos são: CVV; GVV; VV; CV; e GV (onde C = consoante surda e G = consoante sonora). O peso da sílaba se deriva do número das vogais na sílaba e da duração relativa das consoantes: as consoantes surdas são marcadas [+ tenso] e portanto são mais "pesadas" do que as sonoras, que são [- tenso] (cf. Grimês - 1981). (421) xi.'pói.hí CV CVV CV "mulher" ... (422) 'xa.ba.gi CV GV GV "tucano" ... (424) xi.bí.'gaí CV GV GVV "grosso" (425) 'xií.to.ii CVV CV VV "cabo" …
737.idn: Pirahã (língua pirahã), member of the Mura family; the author avoids the label 'mura-pirahã'. Data from the downriver (more acculturated) of the two Pirahã settlements, near the mouth of the Rio Maici.; data: Rio Maici, Amazonas, Brazil; c. 110 speakers, almost 100% monolingual; fieldwork in the village January-March…

737.tone: Pirahã is also tonal: Everett (§22.2.3) analyses two underlying tone levels (a register system, against the three levels of Heinrichs 1964 / Sheldon 1974), marked independently of stress; in morpheme combinations the high tone of a word-final stressed syllable shifts and 'até parece seguir a acentuação' (even seems to follow the stress) (§22.3.3.3).

tn.quote: Heinrichs (1964) e Sheldon (1974) propuseram três níveis fonéticos-fonêmicos de tom para o pirahã. ... um quarto tom fonético ... Este quarto tom, o "baixo baixado" (simbolizado por '+') foi observado. Em segundo lugar, certos processos fonológics foram descritos (ver abaixo), que permitem a postulação de dois, em vez de três, níveis tonais ao nível subjacente. Segundo os critérios classificatórios sugeridos por Pike (1948), o sistema tonal do pirahã seria por registros e não por contornos. ... (onde {H ´} = 'tom alto; {M ¯} = 'tom médio; {L `} = 'tom baixo; e {L+ +} = 'tom baixo baixado')
tn.translation: Heinrichs (1964) and Sheldon (1974) proposed three phonetic-phonemic tone levels for Pirahã. ... a fourth phonetic tone ... This fourth tone, the "lowered low" (symbolized by '+'), was observed. Second, certain phonological processes were described (see below) which allow the postulation of two, instead of three, tone levels at the underlying level. By the classificatory criteria suggested by Pike (1948), the Pirahã tone system would be a register system and not a contour system. ... (where {H ´} = 'high tone; {M ¯} = 'mid tone; {L `} = 'low tone; and {L+ +} = 'lowered low tone')
tn.cite: Everett, Daniel L. 1983. A língua pirahã e a teoria da sintaxe: descrição, perspectivas e teoria. Tese de doutorado, UNICAMP, Campinas.
tn.note: Register tone: 2 underlying levels (H, L), 4 phonetic (adds mid, 'lowered low'); every vowel marked; not lab-verified. Weight-based stress separate; a final H shifts with stress across morphemes.

evidence_works.detail: The paper is about culture and grammar, not phonology; its prosodic content is one summary sentence plus footnotes. It asserts a five-way syllable-weight distinction, which matches the catalog's five syllable types (CVV, GVV, VV, CV, GV), and cites Everett 1979, 1988 and Everett & Everett 1984 (Linguistic Inquiry 15, 'On the relevance of syllable onsets to stress placement') for it. evidence_works.detail: Stress (acentuação): five syllable types CVV, GVV, VV, CV, GV (C = voiceless, G = voiced consonant), ordered on the abscissa of a diagram from CVV (heaviest) to GV (lightest), with linear position (final, penult, antepenult) on the ordinate; 'a acentuação depende primeiramente no tipo de sílaba e secundariamente da posição linear da sílaba' (p. 51-52); the 'regra de atração de acentuação' puts stress on the syllable nearest the end whose mora duration is not exceeded by any other syllable, formalised as rule (7) on p. 53; word-initial voiceless consonants count as longer than any voiced conson

738.heavy: Polański: a syllable with a FULL (non-reduced) vowel ('samogłoska pełna / niezredukowana') vs a reduced vowel; he explicitly denies a long:short vowel opposition. Trubetzkoy 1929 / Olesch / Dogil (StressTyp2's sources): a LONG vowel = bimoraic syllable (full vowels and diphthongs are the long ones); StressTyp2 ': long vowels'.
738.dflt: Not attested: Dogil notes the corpus has no words with both final syllables short; Polański says apparent antepenult-stress forms with two final reduced syllables vanish on re-analysis (p. 38). StressTyp2's 'else initial' default is an artefact with no support in the source.
738.prule: Polański (p. 48): stress fell on the last non-reduced (full-vowel) syllable of the word; since post-tonic vowels are reduced and forms with two final reduced syllables 'disappear on analysis' (p. 38), this is the final syllable if its vowel is full, else the penult. Trubetzkoy/Olesch/Dogil equivalent: stress on the penultimate mora = final syllable if long, else penultimate.
738.srule: Exists, placement not given: Polański only asserts that a secondary stress 'must also have existed' in Polabian ('w języku połabskim musiał występować także akcent poboczny', p. 45, arguing that V-V-V trisyllables could then bear main stress on the first or the last syllable) and reports, without adopting it, Lehr-Spławiński's 1929 view that full vowels stood under main or secondary stress (p. 80). No placement rule is given; Kortlandt 1989 and StressTyp (Dogil 1999; van der Hulst et al. 2010) say nothing about secondary stress.

tn.quote: Z tezą Trubieckiego o morowym charakterze prozodii połabskiej polemizuje Bethin (1998: 181-182) ... Twierdzi ona, że gdyby w języku połabskim przycisk padał na morę, to byłby fonetycznie realizowany jako intonacja a w takim wypadku oczekiwalibyśmy różnic „tonalnych czy innych” między długimi sylabami z akcentem na pierwszej morze ... a sylabami z akcentem na drugiej morze ... Tymczasem w zabytkach połabskich tego typu różnic się nie notuje. ... Można z wysokim prawdopodobieństwem przypuszczać, że nawet gdyby język połabski wykazywał różnice intonacyjne, nie znalazłyby one odbicia w zabytkach.
tn.translation: Bethin (1998: 181-182) argues against Trubetzkoy's thesis of the moraic character of Polabian prosody ... She claims that if in Polabian the stress fell on the mora, it would be realised phonetically as intonation, and in that case we would expect 'tonal or other' differences between long syllables stressed on the first mora ... and syllables stressed on the second mora ... Yet no differences of this kind are recorded in the Polabian texts. ... One may suppose with high probability that even if Polabian had shown intonational differences, they would not have been reflected in the records.

evidence_works.detail: The article restates the accepted phonology the catalog entry rests on (penultimate stress preferred, a heavy final syllable attracts stress, antepenultimate stress lexically exceptional though about 12% of dictionary words, verbs stressed by morphology) and adds phonetic detail: spectral and energy features alone separate stressed from unstressed vowels in continuous speech (word-token accuracy about 93% in the simpler conditions, 69.7% in the hardest), a departure from earlier reports that only duration is robust. It also finds that posttonic vowels are more reliably unstressed than pretonic
evidence_works.loc: p. 7 (Art. 3), section 2.1; results pp. 35-37

evidence_works.work: Veloso 2021, Element Iteration Respecification: Unstressed Word-Final [u] in Portuguese (Linguística: Revista de Estudos Linguísticos da Universidade do Porto N.º Especial: 393-412. doi:10.)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: A theoretical (Element Theory) paper on European Portuguese primary stress: word-final [a], [i] and stressed [u] are treated as inherently heavy stress attractors, while the unstressed final [u] of inflected nouns and adjectives (menino, alto) is the class marker /o/ lexically and so does not attract stress; palatal onsets of the final syllable force penultimate stress. No acoustic data; it adds segment-based weight detail and the three-syllable window to the weight-hedged entry without contradicting it.
evidence_works.loc: pp. 400-401; final remarks p. 409
evidence_works.venue: Linguística: Revista de Estudos Linguísticos da Universidade do Porto

evidence_works.work: Arantes 2021, Effects of speaking style on the shape of fundamental frequency distributions (Revista da ABRALIN 20(1). doi:10.25189/rabralin.v20i1.1800)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: An f0-distribution study of Brazilian Portuguese across speaking styles; it states only that BP word stress is not fixed and can be lexically contrastive, and finds that in isolated word reading speakers align a fast f0 rise or fall with the stressed syllable, which makes most word-reading f0 histograms bimodal. It gives no stress rule and nothing on syllable weight, so it adds an intonational correlate of stress to the entry without touching its position or type; nothing on lexical tone.

evidence_works.work: Post da Silveira 2020, Retrieving L2 word stress from orthography: Evidence from word naming and cross-modal priming (Ilha do Desterro 73(1): 409-441. doi:10.5007/2175-8026.2020v73n1p409)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article summarises Brazilian Portuguese stress from earlier sources as a three-syllable window (final, penultimate, antepenultimate) with penultimate stress predominant, over 70% of 2-4-syllable words, and adds lexical frequency figures for the other positions (the second sentence's 'ultimate and penultimate... 20% and 5%' reads as a slip for ultimate and antepenultimate). Its own experiments are psycholinguistic: bilinguals misplaced stress on 32% of disyllabic words, always toward the final syllable, and more often on cognates whose L1 and L2 stress positions differ.

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Puluwatese; Puluwat: primary stress on the right-most heavy syllable, else on final syllable; secondary stress: Iterative, QS (v6)". The source gives: 'Stress is about even on all syllables', with hedged exceptions: CVCV words 'seem' stressed on the final vowel; h-initial syllables 'usually' stressed (each of them, non-culminatively, e.g. yekúhÚ); excrescent vowels unstressed; 'a number of words' CVCVCV stressed on V1 and V3. — StressTyp2's ingredients (h-initial syllables as 'heavy', CVCV final stress) are on Elbert p.13, but its L/L rule 'right-most heavy syllable, else final' plus iterative QS secondary is an extrapolation the source never states…

ev.cite: Elbert, Samuel H. 1974. Puluwat Grammar. Pacific Linguistics, Series B, No. 29. Canberra: Australian National University. — pp.13-14, ch. 'Phonology', section 'Notes on Stress'
ev.text: Notes on Stress. Stress is about even on all syllables, with these noticeable exceptions (vowels strongly stressed are capitalised; excrescent vowels with weak stress are shown with a brev): (1) CVCV words seem stressed on the final vowels: hanA hibiscus flower, ... yifA? where?, ... yiwE then. (2) Syllables beginning with h- are usually stressed: yapwahAaló to dry out, pahAló to drift away, yekúhÚ rak just a little. (3) The excrescent vowel is weak and unstressed (except after h-). ... (e) A number of words of the shape C1V1C2V2C3V3 have stress on V1 and V3 and weak stress on V2: ...

morph.rootq: "Stress is about even on all syllables, with these noticeable exceptions (vowels strongly stressed are capitalised; excrescent vowels with weak stress are shown with a brev): (1) CVCV words seem stressed on the final vowels: hanA hibiscus flower, kiyÓ outrigger boom, yifA? where?, YisÓ Esau, yiwE then. (2) Syllables beginning with h- are usually stressed: yapwahAaló to dry out, pahAló to drift away, yekúhÚ rak just a little. (3) The excrescent vowel is weak and unstressed (except after h-)." (Elbert 1974:13). The rule is stated over words/syllables, not the root or stem; the only morphology-referring stress remarks are incidental: excrescent (unstressed) vowels occur "Between bases and…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was observed. The 'Notes on Stress' (p.13) simply assert "Stress is about even on all syllables, with these noticeable exceptions (vowels strongly stressed are capitalised ...)" and illustrate with isolated citation words (hanA 'hibiscus flower', kiyÓ 'outrigger boom', yifA? 'where?') plus one two-word phrase (yekúhÚ rak 'just a little'); the following 'Notes on Pitch and Juncture' (p.14) use whole sentences, some cited from the recorded texts (T3:3). Fieldwork context only: "persons who helped in the field in 1967 ... and my Puluwat informant, Tilime" (Preface, p.v).
morph.stmt: Elbert's template (Table 8 'Bases and bound affixes', p.64) is YV1kk- (plural/frequentative) ± Caus yA- ± mE- (quality) + (Redup) + BASE + stem vowel ± Object suffix ± Directional suffix; in his words (p.63): "Already discussed are attributive suffixes, object suffixes, and directional suffixes. Three prefixes, each with allomorphs, are common. They may be symbolized YV1kk-, plural and frequentative; ya-, causative; and me-, quality. Reduplications also are common." I.e. all inflection on nouns and verbs (possessor/construct, object, directionals, plus lexical suffixes -kkit, -lap, -yákin-, -fengann etc.) is suffixal, derivation adds a few prefixes…

740.cfw: Elbert (1974), the only first-hand grammar of Puluwat, describes stress as "about even on all syllables" with only scattered exceptions (final vowel in CVCV words, h-initial syllables) and gives no placement rule, so the record stays undetermined; Elbert's 1972 dictionary and Jackson's 1983 Trukic dissertation say nothing about Puluwat word stress, and StressTyp2's quantity-sensitive coding is a reinterpretation of that same Elbert 1974 passage.

Need more data.' CIDCA 1987 p. vii frames its remark on data from eight speakers ('Los ocho hablantes ramas de quienes fueron recogidos los datos no mostraron grandes diferencias de pronunciacion') without saying whether accent was judged from isolated words or texts; Chevrier 2012 pp. 14-15 says only 'El rama es una lengua con un sistema de acentuacion metrica, tal como lo habia descrito Craig' (Craig 1988a: 41-44).
morph.stmt: Mixed but split by category: person marking (subject prefixes, inalienable possessor prefixes) and postposition-derived preverbs precede the root, while all tense/aspect, modality, subordination and plural marking follows it -- Craig 1986 p.31: 'The fact that all tense/aspects and subordinating morphemes are suffixed to the verb will be considered again...', p.33: 'To be added to the list of word order characteristics of OV languages is the suffixal nature of both the aspect markers and the clause subordinators'; CIDCA 1987 p. viii: verbs 'al hablar se usan con un prefijo que marca la persona y un sufijo que marca tiempo-aspecto como en an-paun-i ellos-llorar-tiempo'.

evidence_works.detail: No positional word-stress rule is stated: Lehmann says word and syllable accent were marked on every word (acute) and in sentence examples, that one- and two-peaked syllable accents and strongly/weakly cut accents occur (the latter not distinguished, since syllable length plus the accent mark shows the facts). Vowel/syllable length is treated as a phonological property (long vs short/half-long syllables, floating diphthongs count as long), but it is coupled to PITCH, not to stress placement, so the entry's weight-hedged kind (heavy = long vowels; closed syllables) is neither confirmed nor cont
